claim: Extensive evidence now underscores the profound impact of species loss on the stability and dynamics of ecosystem functions.
source: Extensive evidence now underscores the profound impact of species loss on the stability and dynamics of ecosystem functions.
evidence: This is a general statement about existing evidence in the field, supported by established scientific consensus.

claim: The absolute effect size of genetic diversity on ecosystem functions mirrors that of species diversity in natural ecosystems.
source: We found that, overall, the absolute effect size of genetic diversity on ecosystem functions mirrors that of species diversity in natural ecosystems.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Genetic diversity was positively correlated with various ecosystem functions.
source: We nonetheless unveil a striking dichotomy: while genetic diversity was positively correlated with various ecosystem functions, species diversity displays a negative correlation with these functions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Species diversity displays a negative correlation with ecosystem functions.
source: We nonetheless unveil a striking dichotomy: while genetic diversity was positively correlated with various ecosystem functions, species diversity displays a negative correlation with these functions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The antagonistic effects of species and genetic diversity persist across the three trophic levels.
source: These intriguing antagonist effects of species and genetic diversity persist across the three trophic levels (underscoring its systemic nature), but were apparent only when BEFs were assessed within trophic levels rather than across them.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The antagonistic effects of species and genetic diversity were apparent only when BEFs were assessed within trophic levels rather than across them.
source: These intriguing antagonist effects of species and genetic diversity persist across the three trophic levels (underscoring its systemic nature), but were apparent only when BEFs were assessed within trophic levels rather than across them.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Diversity within and among species are both important to ensure and stabilize ecosystem functions.
source: Diversity within and among species are both important to ensure and stabilize ecosystem functions (Cardinale et al., 2012; Raffard et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Studies on the links between biodiversity and ecosystem functioning have primarily focused on the interspecific (species) facet of biodiversity.
source: Studies on the links between biodiversity and ecosystem functioning (BEFs) have primarily focused on the interspecific (species) facet of biodiversity (Balvanera et al., 2006; Hooper et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The intraspecific (genetic) facet of biodiversity has been shown to have substantial effects on ecosystem functions.
source: However, the intraspecific (genetic) facet of biodiversity has also recently been shown to have substantial effects on ecosystem functions (Crutsinger et al., 2006; Hughes and Stachowicz, 2004; Reusch et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent meta-analyses have shown that genetic diversity of plant and animal populations affect ecosystem functions.
source: Recent meta-analyses have shown that genetic diversity of plant and animal populations affect ecosystem functions, and that the magnitude (and shape) of intraspecific BEFs is similar to that of species diversity (Raffard et al., 2019; Wan et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous meta-analyses.

claim: The magnitude (and shape) of intraspecific BEFs is similar to that of species diversity.
source: Recent meta-analyses have shown that genetic diversity of plant and animal populations affect ecosystem functions, and that the magnitude (and shape) of intraspecific BEFs is similar to that of species diversity (Raffard et al., 2019; Wan et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous meta-analyses.

claim: Most studies investigating BEFs consider each biodiversity facet separately.
source: Although natural assemblages encompass both intra- and interspecific diversity, most studies investigating BEFs are considering each biodiversity facet separately (but see, Fridley and Grime, 2010; Prieto et al., 2015; Grele et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research and exceptions.

claim: The few studies investigating the combined effects of genetic and species diversity on ecosystem functions were all conducted experimentally under controlled conditions.
source: The few studies investigating the combined effects of genetic and species diversity on ecosystem functions were all conducted experimentally by manipulating the genetic and species diversity of assemblages under controlled conditions (Fridley and Grime, 2010; Hargrave et al., 2011; Prieto et al., 2015; but see Grele et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Environmental variation can either reduce or enhance the effects of biodiversity on ecosystem functions.
source: However, knowledge acquired from BEFs at the interspecific level reveals that environmental variation can either reduce or enhance the effects of biodiversity on ecosystem functions, hence generating large variance in the magnitude and direction of BEFs measured in the wild (Hagan et al., 2021; van der Plas, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Biodiversity at a given trophic level can propagate across trophic levels, generating 'multi-trophic BEFs'.
source: BEF studies often consider a single trophic level, despite accumulating evidence that biodiversity at a given trophic level can propagate across trophic levels, generating 'multi-trophic BEFs' (Lefcheck et al., 2015; Soliveres et al., 2016; Seibold et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Studies testing the joint effects of genetic and species diversity on ecosystem functions have mostly considered the effect of primary producer diversity on their own productivity.
source: In particular, studies testing the joint effects of genetic and species diversity on ecosystem functions have mostly considered the effect of primary producer diversity on their own productivity ('within-trophic level BEFs', e.g. Hargrave et al., 2011; Prieto et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A genetically diverse predator population shares their resources more efficiently than a genetically poor predator population, which might permit a higher prey species coexistence and hence a larger prey biomass.
source: Indeed, it is predicted that a genetically diverse predator population shares their resources more efficiently than a genetically poor predator population, which might permit a higher prey species coexistence and hence a larger prey biomass (between-trophic level BEFs due to genetic diversity, e.g. Raffard et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a prediction based on previous research cited.

claim: A species-rich community of primary producers likely exhibits higher primary production, as organisms in species-rich communities share basal resources more efficiently than in species-poor communities.
source: Alternatively, a species-rich community of primary producers likely exhibits higher primary production, as organisms in species-rich communities share basal resources more efficiently than in species-poor communities (within-trophic level BEFs due to species diversity, Balvanera et al., 2006; Hooper et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: At higher trophic levels, species richness is generally lower.
source: At higher trophic levels (e.g. predators), species richness is generally lower, which should increase the likelihood for genetic diversity (of a few species) to have strong effects on functions.
evidence: This is based on general ecological knowledge.

claim: The study focused on three trophic levels from river ecosystems: riparian trees (primary producers), macroinvertebrate shredders (primary consumers), and fish (secondary consumers).
source: We focused on three trophic levels from river ecosystems; riparian trees (primary producers), macroinvertebrate shredders (primary consumers), and fish (secondary consumers).
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: For each trophic level, the study quantified the species diversity of each community, as well as the genetic diversity of a single target and dominant species.
source: For each trophic level, we quantified the species diversity of each community, as well as the genetic diversity of a single target and dominant species (Alnus glutinosa, Gammarus sp., and Phoxinus dragarum respectively).
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: The study estimated several ecosystem functions, including leave decomposition of riparian trees, biomass of each target species, and total biomass of each community within each trophic level.
source: We further estimated several ecosystem functions, including leave decomposition of riparian trees, biomass (as productivity estimates) of each target species, and total biomass of each community within each trophic level.
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: The percentage of variance in ecosystem function explained by the environment and biodiversity varies from 10% (invertebrate biomass) to 55% (Phoxinus biomass).
source: The percentage of variance in ecosystem function explained by the environment and biodiversity varies from 10% (invertebrate biomass, Figure 3e) to 55% (Phoxinus biomass, Figure 3f) and was moderate overall.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis, referencing specific figures.

claim: For all functions but the three biomass, part of the variance was (directly) explained by at least one out of the two environmental principal component analysis (PCA) axes.
source: For all functions but the three biomass, part of the variance was (directly) explained by at least one out of the two environmental principal component analysis (PCA) axes.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis.

claim: Direct environmental effects on ecosystem functions did not predominate.
source: Overall, direct environmental effects on ecosystem functions did not predominate, and environmental effect sizes were similar (in strength) to that of biodiversity effects, showing the non-negligible role of biodiversity for ecosystem functions in the wild.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis.

claim: Environmental effect sizes were similar (in strength) to that of biodiversity effects.
source: Overall, direct environmental effects on ecosystem functions did not predominate, and environmental effect sizes were similar (in strength) to that of biodiversity effects, showing the non-negligible role of biodiversity for ecosystem functions in the wild.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis.

claim: Individual effect sizes (Zr) measured between BEFs were weak to moderate, irrespective of the considered ecosystem function and of the type of BEFs.
source: Individual effect sizes (Zr) measured between BEFs (biodiversity and ecosystem functions relationships) were weak to moderate, irrespective of the considered ecosystem function and of the type of BEFs (genetic/species BEFs, within-trophic level/between-trophic level BEFs) (Figure 4a and b, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis, referencing specific figures.

claim: BEFs ranged from negative to positive, and their distribution was centered around 0.
source: As expected under natural conditions (Hagan et al., 2021), BEFs ranged from negative to positive, and their distribution was centered around 0, although we observed a slight tendency for genetic BEFs toward positive values (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis, referencing a figure and citing previous research.

claim: Only 4 out of the 34 BEFs were strong and significant.
source: Only 4 out of the 34 BEFs were strong and significant; two significant BEFs concerned species BEFs (negative relationship between the biomass of A. glutinosa and the diversity of trees, Zr = –0.446, 95% CI [–0.695,–0.143]; negative relationship between the biomass of P. dragarum and the diversity of fish, Zr = –0.529, 95% CI [–0.802,–0.166]) and two concerned genetic BEFs (negative relationship between the biomass of P. dragarum and the diversity of A. glutinosa, Zr = –0.321, 95% CI [–0.602,–0.019]; positive relationship between the biomass of Gammarus sp. and the diversity of P. dragarum, Zr = 0.446, 95% CI [0.001, 0.829]) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis, referencing a figure.

claim: There is a negative relationship between the biomass of A. glutinosa and the diversity of trees (Zr = –0.446, 95% CI [–0.695,–0.143]).
source: Only 4 out of the 34 BEFs were strong and significant; two significant BEFs concerned species BEFs (negative relationship between the biomass of A. glutinosa and the diversity of trees, Zr = –0.446, 95% CI [–0.695,–0.143]; negative relationship between the biomass of P. dragarum and the diversity of fish, Zr = –0.529, 95% CI [–0.802,–0.166]) and two concerned genetic BEFs (negative relationship between the biomass of P. dragarum and the diversity of A. glutinosa, Zr = –0.321, 95% CI [–0.602,–0.019]; positive relationship between the biomass of Gammarus sp. and the diversity of P. dragarum, Zr = 0.446, 95% CI [0.001, 0.829]) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: There is a negative relationship between the biomass of P. dragarum and the diversity of fish (Zr = –0.529, 95% CI [–0.802,–0.166]).
source: Only 4 out of the 34 BEFs were strong and significant; two significant BEFs concerned species BEFs (negative relationship between the biomass of A. glutinosa and the diversity of trees, Zr = –0.446, 95% CI [–0.695,–0.143]; negative relationship between the biomass of P. dragarum and the diversity of fish, Zr = –0.529, 95% CI [–0.802,–0.166]) and two concerned genetic BEFs (negative relationship between the biomass of P. dragarum and the diversity of A. glutinosa, Zr = –0.321, 95% CI [–0.602,–0.019]; positive relationship between the biomass of Gammarus sp. and the diversity of P. dragarum, Zr = 0.446, 95% CI [0.001, 0.829]) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: There is a negative relationship between the biomass of P. dragarum and the diversity of A. glutinosa (Zr = –0.321, 95% CI [–0.602,–0.019]).
source: Only 4 out of the 34 BEFs were strong and significant; two significant BEFs concerned species BEFs (negative relationship between the biomass of A. glutinosa and the diversity of trees, Zr = –0.446, 95% CI [–0.695,–0.143]; negative relationship between the biomass of P. dragarum and the diversity of fish, Zr = –0.529, 95% CI [–0.802,–0.166]) and two concerned genetic BEFs (negative relationship between the biomass of P. dragarum and the diversity of A. glutinosa, Zr = –0.321, 95% CI [–0.602,–0.019]; positive relationship between the biomass of Gammarus sp. and the diversity of P. dragarum, Zr = 0.446, 95% CI [0.001, 0.829]) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: There is a positive relationship between the biomass of Gammarus sp. and the diversity of P. dragarum (Zr = 0.446, 95% CI [0.001, 0.829]).
source: Only 4 out of the 34 BEFs were strong and significant; two significant BEFs concerned species BEFs (negative relationship between the biomass of A. glutinosa and the diversity of trees, Zr = –0.446, 95% CI [–0.695,–0.143]; negative relationship between the biomass of P. dragarum and the diversity of fish, Zr = –0.529, 95% CI [–0.802,–0.166]) and two concerned genetic BEFs (negative relationship between the biomass of P. dragarum and the diversity of A. glutinosa, Zr = –0.321, 95% CI [–0.602,–0.019]; positive relationship between the biomass of Gammarus sp. and the diversity of P. dragarum, Zr = 0.446, 95% CI [0.001, 0.829]) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: There is a significant interaction between the facet at which biodiversity is measured (genetic or species diversity), and the type of BEF that was measured (within- or between-trophic levels).
source: We confirmed this visual tendency by summarizing all individual Zr through a meta-regression. Indeed, we found a significant interaction between the facet at which biodiversity is measured (genetic or species diversity), and the type of BEF that was measured (within- or between-trophic levels; Table 1; Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from the meta-regression analysis, referencing tables.

claim: Within-trophic level BEFs were significantly negative when considering species diversity (ZrWithin*Species = –0.185, 95% CI [–0.343,–0.027]).
source: This interaction indicates (i) that – overall – within-trophic level BEFs were significantly negative when considering species diversity (ZrWithin*Species = –0.185, 95% CI [–0.343,–0.027]), whereas within-trophic level BEFs were significantly positive when considering genetic diversity (ZrWithin*Genetic = 0.168, 95% CI [0.010, 0.326], see Figure 5a), and (ii) that this pattern was not observed for between-trophic levels BEFs, where no particular trend was observed (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the meta-regression analysis, referencing a figure.

claim: Within-trophic level BEFs were significantly positive when considering genetic diversity (ZrWithin*Genetic = 0.168, 95% CI [0.010, 0.326]).
source: This interaction indicates (i) that – overall – within-trophic level BEFs were significantly negative when considering species diversity (ZrWithin*Species = –0.185, 95% CI [–0.343,–0.027]), whereas within-trophic level BEFs were significantly positive when considering genetic diversity (ZrWithin*Genetic = 0.168, 95% CI [0.010, 0.326], see Figure 5a), and (ii) that this pattern was not observed for between-trophic levels BEFs, where no particular trend was observed (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the meta-regression analysis, referencing a figure.

claim: No particular trend was observed for between-trophic levels BEFs.
source: This interaction indicates (i) that – overall – within-trophic level BEFs were significantly negative when considering species diversity (ZrWithin*Species = –0.185, 95% CI [–0.343,–0.027]), whereas within-trophic level BEFs were significantly positive when considering genetic diversity (ZrWithin*Genetic = 0.168, 95% CI [0.010, 0.326], see Figure 5a), and (ii) that this pattern was not observed for between-trophic levels BEFs, where no particular trend was observed (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a result from the meta-regression analysis, referencing a figure.

claim: Species diversity is negatively associated with ecosystem functions when the influence of biodiversity on ecosystem functions is measured within the same trophic level.
source: Although most individual Zr were weak to moderate (and not significant), their consistency (in terms of magnitude and direction) resulted in a significant pattern whereby species and genetic diversity have opposite effects on ecosystem functions for within-trophic level BEFs; species diversity is negatively associated, whereas genetic diversity is positively associated with ecosystem functions, but only when the influence of biodiversity on ecosystem functions is measured within the same trophic level.
evidence: This is a synthesized result from the meta-regression analysis.

claim: Genetic diversity is positively associated with ecosystem functions when the influence of biodiversity on ecosystem functions is measured within the same trophic level.
source: Although most individual Zr were weak to moderate (and not significant), their consistency (in terms of magnitude and direction) resulted in a significant pattern whereby species and genetic diversity have opposite effects on ecosystem functions for within-trophic level BEFs; species diversity is negatively associated, whereas genetic diversity is positively associated with ecosystem functions, but only when the influence of biodiversity on ecosystem functions is measured within the same trophic level.
evidence: This is a synthesized result from the meta-regression analysis.

claim: The results confirm a previous meta-analysis demonstrating that genetic and species diversity modulates ecosystem functions with a similar magnitude.
source: Our results confirm a previous meta-analysis demonstrating that genetic and species diversity modulates ecosystem functions with a similar magnitude (Raffard et al., 2019), and results from few experimental studies that manipulated both the genetic and species components of biodiversity under controlled conditions (e.g. Jiang et al., 2022; Prieto et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Within trophic levels, the absolute mean effect size of genetic and species diversity across ecosystem functions were of the same magnitude (|Zr|=0.168 and 0.185 for genetic and species diversity effects respectively).
source: Indeed, within trophic levels, the absolute mean effect size of genetic and species diversity across ecosystem functions were of the same magnitude (|Zr|=0.168 and 0.185 for genetic and species diversity effects respectively), and slightly greater than the effect sizes reported under controlled conditions (|lnRR|=0.132 and 0.134 for genetic and species diversity effects respectively, Raffard et al., 2019) and those more generally reported for species BEFs (|Zr|=0.101, Balvanera et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis, compared with previous research.

claim: The absolute mean effect sizes of genetic and species diversity in this study were slightly greater than the effect sizes reported under controlled conditions (|lnRR|=0.132 and 0.134 for genetic and species diversity effects respectively).
source: Indeed, within trophic levels, the absolute mean effect size of genetic and species diversity across ecosystem functions were of the same magnitude (|Zr|=0.168 and 0.185 for genetic and species diversity effects respectively), and slightly greater than the effect sizes reported under controlled conditions (|lnRR|=0.132 and 0.134 for genetic and species diversity effects respectively, Raffard et al., 2019) and those more generally reported for species BEFs (|Zr|=0.101, Balvanera et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous research cited.

claim: The vast majority (91% of 23 reviewed studies by 2019) of studies investigating the effects of genetic diversity on ecosystem functions have focused on primary producers.
source: As pointed out by Raffard et al., 2019, the vast majority (91% of 23 reviewed studies by 2019, see also Wan et al., 2022) of studies investigating the effects of genetic diversity on ecosystem functions have focused on primary producers, and all of them were based on experiments, which is also the case for most studies manipulating both genetic and species diversity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: All studies investigating the effects of genetic diversity on ecosystem functions were based on experiments.
source: As pointed out by Raffard et al., 2019, the vast majority (91% of 23 reviewed studies by 2019, see also Wan et al., 2022) of studies investigating the effects of genetic diversity on ecosystem functions have focused on primary producers, and all of them were based on experiments, which is also the case for most studies manipulating both genetic and species diversity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The findings provide solid support for broadening the conclusion that both genetic and species diversity can influence ecosystem functions in the wild.
source: On the contrary, our findings provide a solid support for broadening the conclusion that both genetic and species diversity can influence ecosystem functions in the wild.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's results.

claim: For within-trophic level BEFs, the direction of genetic and species effects is opposite; species diversity (in general) reduces the rate of ecosystem functions, whereas genetic diversity enhances the same functions.
source: More strikingly, our results suggest that, although the absolute effect sizes of genetic and species BEFs are of similar magnitude, for within-trophic level BEFs, the direction of their effects is opposite; species diversity (in general) reduces the rate of ecosystem functions, whereas genetic diversity enhances the same functions.
evidence: This is a synthesized result from the data analysis.

claim: Genetic and species diversity have been found to be uncorrelated spatially in this landscape.
source: Moreover (and importantly), as genetic and species diversity have been found to be uncorrelated spatially in this landscape (Fargeot et al., 2023), covariation among diversity estimates cannot explain these patterns.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a companion paper.

claim: Species BEFs were on average negative.
source: Species BEFs were on average negative (see Supplementary file 2 for individual estimates), which contrasts with the general view that species biodiversity favors ecosystem functions, although it is not that surprising (Dee et al., 2023; Hagan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis, with citations to previous research.

claim: The net effect of species biodiversity on ecosystem functions results from the combined effects of both negative factors and positive factors.
source: Indeed, the net effect of species biodiversity on ecosystem functions results from the combined effects of both negative factors, arising from antagonistic interactions such as negative complementarity or negative selection effect, and positive factors, arising from beneficial interactions such as niche complementarity or facilitation (Loreau and Hector, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Intraspecific competition is generally stronger than interspecific competition.
source: Intraspecific competition is generally stronger than interspecific competition (Connell, 1983), and intraspecific interactions could be expected to lead more frequently to negative complementarity (and hence negative genetic BEFs) than interspecific interactions.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Genetic diversity is essential to increase niche complementarity within species and hence to reduce the pervasive effects of intraspecific interactions.
source: Since we observe the opposite, we can hypothesize that genetic diversity is essential to increase niche complementarity within species (Bolnick et al., 2003) and hence to reduce the pervasive effects of intraspecific interactions (Hughes et al., 2008; Prunier et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the study's results and previous research cited.

claim: The antagonistic effects of genetic and species diversity were observed only for BEFs measured within trophic levels, not for those measured between trophic levels.
source: These antagonistic effects were observed only for BEFs measured within trophic levels, not for those measured between trophic levels.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis.

claim: An overall between-trophic level BEF not different from zero suggests that biodiversity at a trophic level has only limited impact on ecosystem functions at another trophic level.
source: An overall between-trophic level BEF not different from zero suggests that biodiversity at a trophic level has only limited impact on ecosystem functions at another trophic level.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's results.

claim: For both genetic and species estimates of biodiversity, there was a substantial variation in effect sizes for between-trophic level BEFs that ranged from negative to positive BEFs.
source: However, for both genetic and species estimates of biodiversity, there was a substantial variation in effect sizes for between-trophic level BEFs that ranged from negative to positive BEFs (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis, referencing a figure.

claim: Biodiversity effects across trophic levels may be more variable in their direction than within-trophic level BEFs.
source: This suggests that biodiversity effects across trophic levels may be more variable in their direction than within-trophic level BEFs, which appear as more constrained.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's results.

claim: The empirical patterns revealed were all extremely consistent across the three trophic levels.
source: The empirical patterns we revealed here were all extremely consistent across the three trophic levels, hence allowing generalization.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis.

claim: BEFs were not particularly stronger at any specific trophic level.
source: It is noteworthy that, although statistically strong and consistent, these patterns must be interpreted with care as field-based approaches are limited in properly taking into account the environmental heterogeneity of natural ecosystems (Hagan et al., 2021). BEFs were not particularly stronger at any specific trophic level and the relative effects of genetic and species diversity were not dependent on the trophic level at which the function was estimated.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis, with a citation to previous research.

claim: The relative effects of genetic and species diversity were not dependent on the trophic level at which the function was estimated.
source: It is noteworthy that, although statistically strong and consistent, these patterns must be interpreted with care as field-based approaches are limited in properly taking into account the environmental heterogeneity of natural ecosystems (Hagan et al., 2021). BEFs were not particularly stronger at any specific trophic level and the relative effects of genetic and species diversity were not dependent on the trophic level at which the function was estimated.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis, with a citation to previous research.

claim: Increased biodiversity loss should have greater consequences for multi-functionality when it occurs at higher trophic levels.
source: We may have expected a stronger top-down regulation (i.e. biodiversity of predators has more effects than biodiversity of preys) of ecosystem functions since previous studies showed that biodiversity loss should have greater consequences for multi-functionality when it occurs at higher trophic levels (Lefcheck et al., 2015; Seibold et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Increased genetic diversity within a predatory fish species has experimentally been shown to indirectly increase the rate of litter decomposition by increasing the diversity of shredders.
source: For instance, increased genetic diversity within a predatory fish species has experimentally been shown to indirectly increase the rate of litter decomposition by increasing the diversity of shredders (Raffard et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The genetic (intraspecific) and species (interspecific) facets of biodiversity are both important drivers of multiple ecosystem functions in a natural and multi-trophic context.
source: To conclude, we found that the genetic (intraspecific) and species (interspecific) facets of biodiversity are both important drivers of multiple ecosystem functions in a natural and multi-trophic context.
evidence: This is a synthesized conclusion from the study's results.

claim: In the wild, genetic and species facets of biodiversity can generate low to moderately high impacts on ecosystem functions measured across three trophic levels.
source: In the wild, these two facets of biodiversity can, as expected, generate low to moderately high impacts on ecosystem functions measured across three trophic levels, and they can operate in opposite directions (but on different functions; genetic diversity is positively associated with some functions, species diversity is negatively associated with other functions).
evidence: This is a synthesized conclusion from the study's results.

claim: Genetic diversity loss often precedes species loss.
source: For instance, genetic diversity loss often precedes species loss, and our results suggest that – in mountain streams – losing genes may actually be particularly detrimental for the performance of ecosystem functions.
evidence: This is based on general ecological knowledge and the study's results.

claim: In mountain streams, losing genes may be particularly detrimental for the performance of ecosystem functions.
source: For instance, genetic diversity loss often precedes species loss, and our results suggest that – in mountain streams – losing genes may actually be particularly detrimental for the performance of ecosystem functions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's results.

claim: The study sampled 52 sites in Southern France from the Adour-Garonne watershed, distributed along an east-west gradient in the Pyrenees Mountains.
source: We sampled 52 sites in Southern France from the Adour-Garonne watershed, and distributed along an east-west gradient in the Pyrenees Mountains (Figure 1a, Blanchet, 2024).
evidence: This describes the study design, referencing a figure.

claim: Riparian trees provide organic matter in the form of fallen leaves as a food source for decomposers.
source: Riparian trees (57 species in the sampled area) provide organic matter in the form of fallen leaves as a food source for decomposers.
evidence: This is based on ecological knowledge.

claim: Alnus glutinosa was selected for acquisition of genetic data due to its dominance at most sites and its functional relevance.
source: We selected the common alder A. glutinosa for acquisition of genetic data due to its dominance at most sites and its functional relevance, as its roots serve as shelters for many aquatic species and are involved in nitrogen fixation.
evidence: This describes the study design rationale.

claim: The roots of Alnus glutinosa serve as shelters for many aquatic species and are involved in nitrogen fixation.
source: We selected the common alder A. glutinosa for acquisition of genetic data due to its dominance at most sites and its functional relevance, as its roots serve as shelters for many aquatic species and are involved in nitrogen fixation.
evidence: This is based on ecological knowledge.

claim: Macroinvertebrate shredders are primary consumers using leaves as resources, and converting them into accessible organic matter for other species.
source: Macroinvertebrate shredders (101 genera in the sampled area) are primary consumers using leaves as resources, and converting them into accessible organic matter for other species.
evidence: This is based on ecological knowledge.

claim: Gammarus sp. is particularly efficient at decomposing tree leaves, in particular those from Alnus.
source: This species is particularly efficient at decomposing tree leaves, in particular those from Alnus (Macneil et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Phoxinus dragarum is an abundant and important predator strongly impacting invertebrate communities.
source: We used the minnow P. dragarum as the fish target species as it is an abundant and important predator strongly impacting invertebrate communities (Raffard et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Fish species number varies from 1 to 11.
source: Fish species number varies from 1 to 11, invertebrate genus number varies from 15 to 42, and the tree species number varies from 7 to 20 (see Fargeot et al., 2023, for details).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data collection.

claim: Invertebrate genus number varies from 15 to 42.
source: Fish species number varies from 1 to 11, invertebrate genus number varies from 15 to 42, and the tree species number varies from 7 to 20 (see Fargeot et al., 2023, for details).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data collection.

claim: Tree species number varies from 7 to 20.
source: Fish species number varies from 1 to 11, invertebrate genus number varies from 15 to 42, and the tree species number varies from 7 to 20 (see Fargeot et al., 2023, for details).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data collection.

claim: A sample size of up to 32 individuals per site was found sufficient for estimating the genomic diversity of populations.
source: At each site, we collected tissue from up to 32 individuals of each of the three target species, a sample size having found sufficient for estimating the genomic diversity of populations (Hale et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The total numbers of SNPs retrieved were 583,862 for A. glutinosa, 331,728 for Gammarus sp., and 414,213 for P. dragarum.
source: The total numbers of SNPs retrieved were 583,862 for A. glutinosa, 331,728 for Gammarus sp., and 414,213 for P. dragarum (see Fargeot et al., 2023, for details).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the genetic data processing.

claim: The Shannon entropy is a metric of evenness that takes into account the distribution of allele or species abundances within each site.
source: The Shannon entropy is a metric of evenness that takes into account the distribution of allele or species abundances within each site (Chao et al., 2014) by weighting each species/allele by its proportional abundance (q=1).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The study measured seven ecosystem functions at each site.
source: At each site, we measured seven ecosystem functions.
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: The study collected biomass production data of all species at each trophic level and the biomass production of each target species as estimates of productivity.
source: We collected biomass production data of all species at each trophic level (hereafter 'total biomass') and the biomass production of each target species as estimates of productivity, as well as the decomposition rate of Alnus leaves.
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: The study measured the decomposition rate of Alnus leaves.
source: We collected biomass production data of all species at each trophic level (hereafter 'total biomass') and the biomass production of each target species as estimates of productivity, as well as the decomposition rate of Alnus leaves.
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: Failing to account for environmental factors may result in overestimated and/or artifactual BEFs.
source: A major challenge for inferring BEFs from empirical data is to take into account the direct and indirect (through biodiversity) effects of environmental factors on ecosystem functions (Duffy et al., 2016; Duffy et al., 2017). Failing to do this may result in overestimated and/or artifactual BEFs, especially if the same environmental factor simultaneously affects biodiversity and ecosystem processes (Grace et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The study measured 13 variables related to river topography and physico-chemical characteristics.
source: For each site, we measured 13 variables related to river topography and physico-chemical characteristics that likely influence biodiversity and ecosystem processes (Altermatt, 2013).
evidence: This describes the study design, with a citation to previous research.

claim: A PCA combining all 13 environmental variables was performed, and coordinates of each site on the two first axes (38.03% of the total variance) were used as two synthetic environmental variables for further analyses.
source: A PCA combining all 13 variables was performed using the R package 'ade4' (Dray and Dufour, 2007), and coordinates of each site on the two first axes (38.03% of the total variance, see Table 1) were used as two synthetic environmental variables for further analyses.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method, referencing a table.

claim: The first PCA axis is defined by a strong contribution of oxygen concentration and altitude.
source: The first axis is defined by a strong contribution of (in decreasing order) oxygen concentration and altitude (Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the PCA analysis, referencing a table.

claim: The second PCA axis is defined by a strong contribution of east-west gradient and connectivity.
source: The second axis is defined by a strong contribution of east-west gradient and connectivity (Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the PCA analysis, referencing a table.

claim: pSEM allows modeling direct and indirect causal relationships among a set of response variables and predictors.
source: pSEM allows modeling direct and indirect causal relationships among a set of response variables and predictors (Shipley, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: pSEM uses local estimates of each linear structural equation separately, which allows the inclusion of a large number of parameters despite modest sample sizes.
source: Further, pSEM uses local estimates of each linear structural equation separately (i.e. parameters are estimated from a series of independent models forming a general causal graph), which allows the inclusion of a large number of parameters despite modest sample sizes (Shipley, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The study ran a pSEM for each ecosystem function separately (seven pSEMs).
source: We ran a pSEM for each ecosystem function separately (i.e. seven pSEMs, see an example in Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method, referencing a figure.

claim: 34 BEFs (out of the 42 possible links) were included in the meta-regression.
source: For some functions (in particular those associated with plant biomass), irrelevant biodiversity-functions links were not included (e.g. the impact of fish or invertebrate diversity on tree biomasses), which results in 34 BEFs (out of the 42 possible links) having been included in the meta-regression (see hereafter).
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method.

claim: The study used a linear mixed model to test whether the magnitude and direction of genetic BEFs are similar to those of species BEFs.
source: We used a linear mixed model to test (i) whether the magnitude and direction of genetic BEFs are similar to those of species BEFs, and (ii) whether within-trophic level BEFs are similar in effect size to between-trophic level BEFs.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method.

claim: The study used a linear mixed model to test whether within-trophic level BEFs are similar in effect size to between-trophic level BEFs.
source: We used a linear mixed model to test (i) whether the magnitude and direction of genetic BEFs are similar to those of species BEFs, and (ii) whether within-trophic level BEFs are similar in effect size to between-trophic level BEFs.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method.
